name: Delayed coking and fluid coking
applications: petroleum coke for fuel or anodes
principle: Vacuum residue is heated quickly in a furnace to 480 to 590 °C and sent to a coke drum at about 400 °C and 25 to 30 psig, where it cracks thermally over many hours. Vapours go to a fractionator, and solid coke builds up in the drum. Drums run in pairs on a semi-batch cycle of 28 to 36 hours, with one filling while the other is steamed, cooled and cut out with high-pressure water.

source.note: US EPA AP-42 Section 5.1 Petroleum Refining (April 2015 revision), process descriptions

performance.basis: EPA AP-42 description, start of feed to start of next feed to the same drum

source.note: US EPA AP-42 Section 5.1 Petroleum Refining (April 2015 revision), process descriptions

advantages: Robust destruction of the heaviest residues
Lower pressure and hydrogen demand than resid hydrocracking
limitations: Drum cycling and decoking are safety-critical
